In all three regimes, small seeds delayed rain slightly and large seeds brought it forward substantially. Each curve crossed zero once, and \(D_c\) decreased in the order maritime > continental > urban. The ordering and direction match the paper; the values are consistently about 0.5 times smaller. The causes of the factor 0.5 (single-mode background, no sedimentation, idealized thermodynamics, unit collision efficiency) are hypotheses that were not tested separately. Because the diameter grid has 1 µm spacing between 1 and 10 µm, \(D_c\) is uncertain by roughly one grid cell. Continental is interpolated between 1 and 2 µm, urban between 0.9 and 1.0 µm, and the maritime mean was exactly zero at 3 µm. A separate urban-only run with 50 members also gave \(D_c\) of about 1.0 µm.
The flattening above 20 µm is a limit of the metric, not physics. From 40 µm upward, onset occurred at 10.5 min in all three regimes, which is the first output just after injection begins. The seeds were counted as rain the moment they arrived. Physical interpretation is therefore restricted to \(D \lesssim 10\) µm, and the paper’s 60 µm optimum cannot be judged by this experiment.

A negative (suppression) paper value counts as agreement when \(\Delta t_{onset}>0\), and a positive (enhancement) value when \(\Delta t_{onset}<0\). All three mismatches sit near the transition. Maritime 2 µm gave a +0.6 min delay (confidence interval ±0.45 min) where Table 2 reports +0.72%. Maritime 3 µm had a mean of exactly zero and was not counted as agreement. Urban 1 µm gave −0.1 min (±0.9 min), effectively zero, where Table 2 reports −4.78%. The 7 further cases dropped by the strict criterion were 0.1 µm in all three regimes, urban 0.4, 0.5, and 0.9 µm, and maritime 4 µm, where the mean shift was smaller than its confidence interval.






WarningWhy the count was redone



The count in the lab-meeting supplementary material treated the maritime 3 µm tie as agreement and mixed in urban results from the separate 50-member run. The 78/81 and 71/81 in this post were recounted on a single 20-member set, without the tie.
Table 2 also reports the paper’s main experiment set (one background). For maritime and continental, the reference sign is therefore borrowed from that set; the regime-specific comparison is the one through \(D_c\). For example, the maritime 2 µm delay disagrees with Table 2 but lies below the paper’s maritime \(D_c\) (about 6 µm), so it points the same way as the paper’s maritime result.








NotePoints that stood out when reading the paper



The paper calls the background of the Table 2 set urban in Section 3.1 but continental (C series) in Section 4.5. Its transition (1→2 µm) matches the urban \(D_c\) (about 2 µm), so this replication reads it as urban. The target \(N_{d,max}\) also differs between Section 2.2 (140/400/1400 cm⁻³) and Section 4.5 (120/450/1400 cm⁻³); the Section 4.5 values were used here. Parts of Section 4.5 say “critical radius”, but the Figure 11 caption and the conclusions use diameter, so it is read as a diameter.

title: Experiment 7. Reproducing the Particle-Size Effect of Ren et al. (2025) in a 0-D Parcel
text:
What did not reproduce

Rain amount. Maximum rain water is structurally flat; the parcel has no counterpart to the paper’s −82 to +192%.
Size dependence within the submicron range. The paper’s strongest suppression is at 0.1 µm, but in the parcel 0.1 µm gave the smallest delay (+0.1 to +0.3 min), with confidence intervals including zero in all three regimes.
The ultragiant optimum. It cannot be judged because of the metric saturation described above.

title: Experiment 7. Reproducing the Particle-Size Effect of Ren et al. (2025) in a 0-D Parcel
section: v2: switching on realistic collisions removed the transition curve
text:
v2: switching on realistic collisions removed the transition curve
The v1 Geometric kernel sets collision and coalescence efficiencies to 1, which makes collisions easier than in reality. A v2 closer to the paper’s bin model was therefore built. The collision kernel was either Hydrodynamic (collision efficiency < 1) or Geometric, and both variants switched on Berry1967 coalescence efficiency and collisional breakup (Straub2010Nf fragmentation) (Jong et al. 2023). It was tested only as a preview: urban, 8 diameters, 4 members.
The outcome was a dichotomy. At every updraft tested (3 m/s for the Hydrodynamic variant, 1.0/1.5/2.0 m/s for the Geometric variant), the control produced no rain at all. Rain appeared only when the seeds themselves were already large (≥ 30 µm for the Geometric variant, ≥ 10 µm for the Hydrodynamic variant), and with no control onset to compare against, no transition curve could be defined. This was interpreted as the parcel lacking what lets real clouds pass the autoconversion bottleneck (long residence time, cloud depth, mixing), but that interpretation was not tested either. v2 was stopped here. In other words, the smooth transition curve of v1 has been shown only under the unit-efficiency assumption.

title: Experiment 7. Reproducing the Particle-Size Effect of Ren et al. (2025) in a 0-D Parcel
text:
Next step: a 1-D column
The next step is a PySDM Kinematic1D column with sedimentation and accumulated surface precipitation. That would, for the first time, produce a quantity of the same kind as the paper’s “Precipitation Variation (%)”, and show whether the control can rain with realistic collision efficiency. Coding has started, but the control column does not yet sustain cloud and rain, so there are no results. The main effort has since moved to WRF, and this work is currently paused.

Conclusion. Even in a 0-D PySDM parcel, the diameter of equal-mass KCl seeds decided whether rain onset was delayed or advanced, and the critical diameter followed the paper’s ordering, maritime ≈ 3.0 > continental ≈ 1.7 > urban ≈ 1.0 µm (paper: 6/3/2 µm). Sign agreement was 78/81 (strict 71/81). The transition, however, was shown only under unit collision efficiency, and rain amount cannot be reproduced by the parcel’s structure.

title: Experiment 5. Updraft and Injection Timing Decide Enhancement or Suppression
text:
NoteProvenance



This experiment was performed outside PySDM-Seeding-Lab. Separate PySDM parcel scripts written in Visual Studio Code were run in parallel with 20 workers on the laboratory server. These are not Seeding Lab results.

title: Experiment 5. Updraft and Injection Timing Decide Enhancement or Suppression
section: Question: why does the same seeding reduce rain in some clouds?
text:
Question: why does the same seeding reduce rain in some clouds?
Experiment 4 found a monotonic picture for one background and one updraft: larger κ, larger dry radius, and later injection gave a stronger response. It ended with three open items: a fair dose definition, background aerosol, and an injection coordinate tied to cloud state instead of absolute time. This experiment takes them up together with updraft strength.

What sets the sign of the seeding effect (enhancement or suppression): seed size, updraft, or injection timing?
Does “suppression” under a strong updraft mean little rain?
If the seed recipe is fixed and only the environment changes, what does the sign map look like?

title: Experiment 5. Updraft and Injection Timing Decide Enhancement or Suppression
section: Design: one experiment varies the recipe, the other varies the environment
text:
Design: one experiment varies the recipe, the other varies the environment









Recipe experiment
Environment experiment




Varied
background × updraft × injection timing × seed dry radius × dose
initial RH × updraft × background × thermodynamic state


Levels
clean 50 / polluted 1,000 mg⁻¹; peak 0.5 / 5 m s⁻¹; 2–4 / 15–20 min; 0.1 / 1 / 5 µm; low / medium / high
90 / 95 / 99%; 0.5 / 2 / 5 m s⁻¹; 50 / 200 / 1,000 mg⁻¹; 300 K·1000 hPa / 290 K·900 hPa / 280 K·800 hPa


Fixed
300 K, 1000 hPa, water vapour 22.2 g kg⁻¹
seed dry radius 1 µm, κ 0.8, medium dose, injection at 2–4 min


Scenarios
72 seeded + 4 controls
81 environments × (seeded + control)


Repetitions × scenarios
10 × 76 = 760 runs
5 × 162 = 810 runs



Common settings: a PySDM 0-D adiabatic parcel (Bartman et al. 2022), condensation + coalescence (geometric kernel; every collision coalesces), Rogers–Yau terminal velocity, Δt 10 s, 40-min integration, 4,096 background + 2,048 seed super-droplets. The background aerosol is lognormal with mode dry radius 75 nm, σg 1.6, κ 0.5; seeds use σg 1.2, κ 0.8. There is no sedimentation and no breakup. Each seeded run is paired with a control through the same random seed.

Dose was matched by dry volume
\[
N_{seed}(r_d)=N_{ref}\left(\frac{1\ \mu\text{m}}{r_d}\right)^{3},\qquad N_{ref}=1,\ 10,\ 100\ \text{mg}^{-1}
\]
\(N_{seed}\) is the number of seed particles per mg of dry air, \(r_d\) the seed median dry radius, and \(N_{ref}\) the number at the 1 µm reference (low/medium/high). One particle’s volume scales with \(r_d^3\), so reducing the number as \(r_d^{-3}\) keeps the total dry volume (the amount of material) the same for every size. Fine seeds (0.1 µm) are therefore 1,000 times more numerous than coarse seeds (1 µm), and giant seeds (5 µm) are 1/125 as numerous. This avoids the fixed-number confusion where size and dose change together.


The updraft is a 12.5-minute pulse
\[
w(t)=\begin{cases}
w_{min}+\left(w_{peak}-w_{min}\right)\sin^{2}\!\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{T}\right) & 0\le t\le T=12.5\ \text{min} \\[4pt]
w_{min} & t>T
\end{cases}
\]
\(w_{peak}\) is the peak updraft and \(w_{min}=0.025\) m s⁻¹ the very weak ascent left after the pulse. The \(\sin^2\) term makes the updraft start from the minimum, peak at 6.25 min, and return to the minimum at 12.5 min. Over 40 min the parcel rises about 0.24 km at 0.5 m s⁻¹ and about 1.9 km at 5 m s⁻¹. Early active (2–4 min) injects while the updraft is growing; late quiescent (15–20 min) injects into an almost stationary parcel after the pulse.


Metric: maximum rain water before 6 mm
Rain means drops with wet radius ≥ 40 µm. The main metric is the difference in maximum rain-water mixing ratio before 6 mm, \(\Delta RWC_{max}\), between seeded and control runs. Without sedimentation or breakup, a large drop never leaves the parcel and keeps collecting others. All 380 strong-updraft runs of the recipe experiment saw their largest drop exceed 6 mm radius between 16 and 27 min, and by 40 min it had grown to about 3 cm radius. No weak-updraft run crossed 6 mm. Where the 6 mm number comes from is the subject of Experiment 6. Using the whole-run maximum instead of the 6 mm cut kept the sign in 71 of 72 recipes.
The two experiments classify sign slightly differently. The recipe experiment uses the sign of the 10-member mean \(\Delta RWC_{max}\); “neutral” only means neither seeded nor control produced rain. The environment experiment scores each pair +1 (enhancement), −1 (suppression), or 0 (no rain in either), and calls the 5-member mean enhancement above +0.2 and suppression below −0.2.

title: Experiment 5. Updraft and Injection Timing Decide Enhancement or Suppression
section: Result 1. Updraft sets the amount of rain
text:
Result 1. Updraft sets the amount of rain



Control maximum rain water (bars) and seeded values (markers) in both experiments. Strong-updraft controls hold two orders of magnitude more rain water than weak-updraft controls.


In the environment experiment, the clean-background control’s maximum rain water before 6 mm grew from 0.04 → 1.39 → 3.73 g kg⁻¹ as the updraft went from 0.5 → 2 → 5 m s⁻¹. A parcel that rises higher simply condenses more water. “Suppression” under a strong updraft therefore does not mean a dry cloud. It means the seeded run is slightly below a control that already makes more than 4 g kg⁻¹ of rain water. In the recipe experiment, strong-updraft seeded − control differences ranged from −5.5% to +1.4% of the control.

The last column counts, among scenarios with a non-zero mean, those in which at least 9 of 10 repetitions had the same sign as the mean.



Seeded − control difference by dose and seed size in the four updraft × timing panels. Colour is seed size (fine 0.1, coarse 1, giant 5 µm dry radius); small circles are the clean and small squares the polluted background; large dots and lines are the mean of the two.



Strong + early: 16 of 18 were suppression. The only exceptions were the two low-dose fine-seed cases (clean +0.035, polluted +0.003 g kg⁻¹). Fine seeds delayed rain onset by 0.7–7.8 min (Δonset > 0 = later), while giant seeds advanced onset by 1.7–5.7 min yet still ended slightly below the control maximum.
Strong + late: all 18 were enhancement, but no larger than 1.4% of the control. Read the warning below.
Weak + early: all 12 coarse and giant cases were enhancement. The polluted control produced no rain at all, but coarse and giant seeds did. Fine seeds removed even the weak rain of the clean control (3 suppression) and left the polluted case rainless on both sides (3 neutral).
Weak + late: all 6 giant cases were enhancement; coarse and fine were small suppression or neutral.







WarningReading the strong + late “all enhancement”




The analysis window is short. The pre-6-mm window of the controls ends at about 18 min (clean) and 21 min (polluted), so seeds injected from 15 min have only a few minutes to affect the metric.
Runs already differed before injection. Despite the shared random seed, seeded runs were not identical to the control before injection (rain-water difference at 14.5 min: clean +0.0035, polluted −0.0006 g kg⁻¹; cause not identified). The clean giant-seed low and medium doses (+0.0035, +0.0046 g kg⁻¹) are about that size, so their sign is not trustworthy.

Of 81 environments, 22 were enhancement, 50 suppression, and 9 neutral. The 9 neutral cases are not cancelling effects: at RH 90% and 0.5 m s⁻¹ neither seeded nor control runs produced rain. The four enhancement cases at 2 m s⁻¹ all occurred at RH 90–95% with moderate or polluted backgrounds and thermodynamic states of 290 K or cooler. Changing only the background, at fixed RH and thermodynamic state, never flipped the sign at 0.5 or 5 m s⁻¹. Background aerosol adjusted the size of the effect rather than its sign.
This experiment used early injection (2–4 min) only. “Strong updraft = suppression” is therefore the same statement as strong + early in the recipe experiment, not a claim about late injection.

Fewer background particles → fewer cloud droplets (recipe-experiment control maximum at 5 m s⁻¹: about 56 vs 990 cm⁻³) → the same water is shared by fewer drops, which grow faster → collision–coalescence starts earlier. At 0.5 m s⁻¹, rain formed only at RH 99%. At 5 m s⁻¹, however, the maximum rain water was nearly identical. In this parcel, a clean background made rain sooner, not more. Rain onset here is the first time rain water exceeds 10⁻⁵ g kg⁻¹, not the start of surface rainfall.

title: Experiment 5. Updraft and Injection Timing Decide Enhancement or Suppression
section: One pair on a Skew-T: seeding barely touched the thermodynamics
text:
One pair on a Skew-T: seeding barely touched the thermodynamics



One control–seeded pair at 300 K·1000 hPa, RH 95%, moderate background, 5 m s⁻¹, fixed recipe. Left: parcel path; right: seeded − control temperature and dew-point differences in mK.


The parcel rose from 1000 hPa to about 794 hPa (about 1.93 km), mostly during the updraft pulse. The seeded − control temperature difference stayed between −21 and +2 mK, only thousandths of a degree. The seeding response lives in the drop size distribution, not in parcel thermodynamics. Because the updraft is prescribed, even this tiny difference cannot feed back into buoyancy or ascent. In this pair the seeded run started rain one minute earlier (8.0 vs 9.0 min) but reached a 0.15% lower maximum rain water, so it sits in a “suppression” cell of the sign map. Onset time and maximum answer different questions. The diagram shows a parcel path, not an environmental sounding, so it cannot diagnose CAPE or CIN.

title: Experiment 5. Updraft and Injection Timing Decide Enhancement or Suppression
section: What can and cannot be said
text:
What can and cannot be said







Category
Content




Supported (sign, consistent across repetitions)
Updraft × timing sets the sign (strong + early suppression 16/18, weak + early enhancement 12/18) · with a fixed early recipe, 50 of 54 environments at 2–5 m s⁻¹ were suppression · absolute rain water is controlled by the updraft · clean backgrounds start rain earlier


Descriptive (magnitude)
\(\Delta RWC_{max}\) values, relative changes, rankings of “strongest” conditions — convergence in super-droplet number and timestep was not checked


Not shown
Surface rainfall (no sedimentation) · cloud invigoration (prescribed updraft, so no latent heat → buoyancy → updraft feedback) · drops beyond 6 mm · results with collision efficiency or breakup · the suppression mechanism (vapour competition and similar ideas are hypotheses)




Conclusion. The sign of the seeding response was set first by the combination of updraft and injection timing, before seed size. Early injection into a strong updraft gave suppression in 16 of 18 recipes, late injection gave enhancement in all 18 (but at most 1.4% of the control), and coarse or giant seeds injected early into a weak updraft always enhanced. “Suppression” here does not mean little rain; it means slightly below a control that already rains a lot.

Every conclusion above stands on the “before 6 mm” cut. That 6 mm comes from the upper limit of a terminal-velocity lookup table, and terminal velocity enters the collision kernel directly. Does the sign pattern survive if the terminal-velocity formula changes?
Continue to Experiment 6

title: Experiment 3. Warm Hygroscopic Seeding Across Background Aerosol Environments
text:
NoteProvenance



This experiment was performed outside PySDM-Seeding-Lab. Independent PySDM scripts were developed in Visual Studio Code and executed in parallel on the laboratory server.

title: Experiment 3. Warm Hygroscopic Seeding Across Background Aerosol Environments
text:
Why add realistic background environments?
Experiment 2 found stronger responses for larger dry radius, higher κ, and later injection, but used one idealized background and a fixed number of seeded particles. Background aerosol controls vapour competition, while fixed particle number and fixed dry mass ask different efficiency questions.
This experiment asks whether the warm-hygroscopic pathway persists across environments, whether response speed and strength differ, whether large particles remain favorable at fixed mass, and whether the best injection stage depends on the background cloud.



Environment

κ

The seeding grid used dry radii of 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, and 3.0 µm; κ of 0.8, 1.0, and 1.2; and injection windows of 10–15, 15–20, 20–25, and 25–30 min. Main runs used collision ON, with representative collision-OFF controls, and a 50-member ensemble.
Fixed number injects the same particle count at every dry radius, so particle size and total dry mass change together. Fixed mass holds total dry material constant, reducing particle number as radius increases. The latter is closer to a material-limited efficiency question.

title: Experiment 3. Warm Hygroscopic Seeding Across Background Aerosol Environments
section: A common pathway, different response regimes
text:
A common pathway, different response regimes



Fixed-number mechanism time series for the three environments.


After injection, water vapour and RH/supersaturation decreased while temperature increased. Water moved into cloud and all-activated particle mass, then into rain water through collision/coalescence. This directional pathway appeared in all three backgrounds.
Under the representative fixed-number condition, clean marine responded first and most strongly. Its low background concentration reduced vapour competition. Polluted conditions were more parameter dependent because many background particles competed for vapour.
Fixed-mass runs retained the same pathway but showed weaker responses overall. Increasing dry radius reduced the number of injected particles, exposing a size–number trade-off. “Larger is better” therefore applies only to the fixed-number comparison.

title: Experiment 3. Warm Hygroscopic Seeding Across Background Aerosol Environments
section: Heatmaps and rankings answer different questions
text:
Heatmaps and rankings answer different questions



Integrated positive response across environment, mass rule, κ, dry radius, and injection time.


integrated_positive_mean combines positive-response magnitude and duration. Early injections have more time to accumulate area, so the metric was paired with last_finite_mean, the response at the last valid simulation time. This matters because some collision-ON members can stop early after generating extremely large particles. Last-finite value, integrated response, median/IQR, and finite fraction must be interpreted together.



Conditions ranked by integrated positive and last-finite rain-water response.


Clean marine was fastest in the representative time series, yet warm-orographic cases occupied many top positions across the full grid. The views are not contradictory: one compares environments at one representative setting; the other searches all parameter combinations.

Clean marine: a fast-response regime
Warm orographic: a conditional amplification regime under large radius and late injection
Polluted continental: a strongly parameter-dependent regime

Clean marine responded strongly around 20–25 min, while warm-orographic top conditions favored 25–30 min injection. Optimal timing reflects environment-specific cloud development rather than a universal “later is better” rule.

title: Experiment 3. Warm Hygroscopic Seeding Across Background Aerosol Environments
section: Microphysical response is not operational suitability
text:
Microphysical response is not operational suitability
This parcel experiment measures internal microphysical rain-water response. Operational targeting also depends on predictability, lifetime, precipitation delivery, and water-resource value. A fast marine response is not automatically the best operational target. Many real orographic programs also involve mixed-phase or glaciogenic—not warm-hygroscopic—seeding, so this result cannot be generalized to all mountain-cloud seeding.

Conclusion. The warm-hygroscopic pathway persisted across all three backgrounds, but its strength and timing were environment dependent. Large particles were favorable at fixed number, while fixed mass exposed a size–number trade-off. Efficiency cannot be reduced to particle size alone.

Top-ranked conditions still require robust checks of median, IQR, finite fraction, and early-stop fraction. Experiment 4 next fixes the background and maps the κ–radius–timing interaction densely.

title: Experiment 1. How Much Does Super-Droplet Resolution Change the Result?
text:
NoteProvenance



This experiment was not run in PySDM-Seeding-Lab. It was an independent PySDM study developed in Visual Studio Code and executed on the laboratory server. It later informed the numerical-qualification design of the Seeding Lab.

title: Experiment 1. How Much Does Super-Droplet Resolution Change the Result?
section: Question: is one large response a physical signal?
text:
Question: is one large response a physical signal?
PySDM represents populations of real particles with super-droplets. n_sd_initial and n_sd_seeding therefore control more than runtime: they determine how finely the background aerosol distribution, seeded-particle distribution, and stochastic collision pairing are represented.
The first collision ON/OFF comparison used 1,000 for both counts. A single resolution and random seed could not tell us whether a rain-water spike was reproducible or merely a coarse-sampling event. This experiment varies numerical representation, not physical seeding dose.

title: Experiment 1. How Much Does Super-Droplet Resolution Change the Result?
text:
Design
n_sd_initial = 1,000 / 2,500 / 5,000 / 10,000
n_sd_seeding = 1,000 / 2,500 / 5,000 / 10,000
Formulae seed = 100–149
rain-size threshold = wet radius 25 µm
The 4 × 4 grid was repeated with 50 random seeds. Seeding-minus-no-seeding differences were evaluated separately with collision ON and OFF. Instead of selecting one curve, the analysis compared ensemble mean and standard deviation, final/maximum/minimum response, positive and negative integrated area, and the full time series.
An early version increased both super-droplet counts together. That mixed changes in background sampling, seeded-particle sampling, and collision-pair sampling. Crossing the two axes independently was the essential correction.

title: Experiment 1. How Much Does Super-Droplet Resolution Change the Result?
section: Collision OFF produced no rain-size response
text:
Collision OFF produced no rain-size response
Rain-water difference remained nearly zero across every collision-OFF combination. Seeded particles could still take up vapour, but condensation alone did not create a measurable increase above the 25 µm wet-radius threshold in this parcel and time window.
With collision ON, both positive spikes and negative responses appeared just after injection. The perturbation was transient rather than a one-way enhancement. Final values and post-20-minute means were generally close to zero, so this experiment does not establish persistent rain-water enhancement.

title: Experiment 1. How Much Does Super-Droplet Resolution Change the Result?
text:
Background representation controlled the variability



Maximum and minimum rain-water response across the two representation axes.


The largest ensemble response and spread occurred at n_sd_initial = 1,000. When the background distribution is represented by fewer computational particles, each super-droplet carries more real-particle weight and an individual collision event can dominate a threshold-based diagnostic.
Increasing n_sd_initial to 2,500, 5,000, and 10,000 generally reduced the magnitude of maximum/minimum response, integrated positive/negative area, and ensemble spread. Changes in n_sd_seeding were weaker. In this configuration, the resolution of the existing cloud-droplet population mattered more than the resolution of the injected population.



Seeding-minus-control ensemble time series. Blue shading is one standard deviation; vertical shading marks the 15–20 min injection window.


Of 1,600 planned collision-setting comparison outputs, 1,599 completed. One collision-ON member at n_sd_initial = 1,000, n_sd_seeding = 5,000 generated an exceptionally large particle and exceeded an interpolation limit. It is retained as evidence of an outlier mechanism rather than silently discarded.

title: Experiment 1. How Much Does Super-Droplet Resolution Change the Result?
text:
Interpretation
A larger spike is not equivalent to stronger seeding. Lower resolution produced larger spikes and greater seed-to-seed variability. Likewise, raising n_sd_seeding does not add more seeding material; it changes the computational representation of the same population.
The 25 µm rain threshold is useful but sensitive to threshold crossing. A stronger follow-up should inspect multiple thresholds, wet-radius spectra, and robust ensemble statistics such as median and IQR.

Conclusion. Collision ON produced transient rain-water perturbations, not a persistent increase. Response magnitude and uncertainty were more sensitive to n_sd_initial than to n_sd_seeding, so a single resolution and random seed cannot support a generalized seeding claim.

The next step fixes numerical resolution and varies physical particle properties in Experiment 2.

title: Qualifying Rain-Producing Experiments and Letting the Server Work Overnight
text:
The previous development connected diagnostic provenance, water budgets, wet-radius spectra, numerical qualification, and reproducible reports. Its qualification profile, however, had collision OFF and zero rain diagnostics. The Lab could explain where a result came from, but it had not yet established what could be trusted in a collision-ON, rain-producing experiment.
PySDM-Seeding-Lab PR #4, merged on 16 July 2026, closes that gap and makes long experiments durable on a Linux lab server. Seven commits changed 42 files, adding 4,808 lines and deleting 141 across qualification, ensemble resource control, detached jobs, and bounded multi-core sweeps.

title: Qualifying Rain-Producing Experiments and Letting the Server Work Overnight
section: A convergence design that runs only the comparisons it needs
text:
A convergence design that runs only the comparisons it needs
The earlier Cartesian grid combined three levels of timestep, background super-droplet count, and seeding super-droplet count: 27 cases and 54 control/seeding executions. Yet the convergence decision only needs one axis varied at a time while the others remain at the finest reference.
The new one_factor_at_reference design runs one reference plus two lower levels on each of three numerical axes: 7 cases and 14 physical executions. It removes 20 combinations that never enter a next-finest convergence comparison without removing any required evidence.
The rain_standard profile used a 5 s reference timestep and 400 background and seeding super-droplets, with condensation and collision ON and sedimentation OFF. All 7 cases and 14 real PySDM executions succeeded in 699 seconds.

rain_response_pilot raised the reference to 800 background and seeding super-droplets, retained the 5 s timestep, and used three common seeds. All 12 case-seed pairs and 24 control/seeding executions completed in 956.4 seconds.
Every run now preserves member-level scalar metrics, paired_seed_metrics.csv, complete case × seed coverage, per-seed rain gates, and per-seed convergence evidence. An unrelated seed or a case mean can never silently substitute for a missing pair.

title: Qualifying Rain-Producing Experiments and Letting the Server Work Overnight
section: Experiments that survive a browser disconnect
text:
Experiments that survive a browser disconnect
Long calculations can now be submitted as detached worker processes from the Run page. Each job stores an immutable YAML snapshot, job ID, PID, queued/running/succeeded/failed state, current stage, completed and total model-run counts, worker log, error, and final result directory under .runtime/jobs/.
A refresh, browser disconnect, or Streamlit rerun no longer terminates the experiment. The new Server Jobs page reconstructs progress and failure evidence from disk.
The web service itself is managed through a headless nohup script:
bash scripts/server_web.sh start
bash scripts/server_web.sh status
bash scripts/server_web.sh stop
bash scripts/server_web.sh restart
It binds to 127.0.0.1:8501 by default and documents SSH tunneling, avoiding direct exposure of an unauthenticated Streamlit service. Restarting the web service does not cancel already detached simulation workers.

title: Qualifying Rain-Producing Experiments and Letting the Server Work Overnight
section: Bound parallelism by cases and memory, not CPU count
text:
Bound parallelism by cases and memory, not CPU count
Independent sweep cases can use a spawn-based process pool configured with execution.max_workers. Ensemble members inside one case remain sequential to avoid nested oversubscription. Effective concurrency is:
min(execution.max_workers, number of sweep cases)
The marine showcase has ten cases, so twenty configured workers cannot create more than ten concurrent case workers. Because one isolated child peaked near 1.03 GiB in the tested profile, the recommended rollout starts at four workers, inspects htop, free -h, and resource evidence, then increases to eight or ten. Twenty workers require more than 20 GiB plus operating-system and application overhead. The project-wide default remains one.
Concurrent timing-history updates now use an inter-process lock, stale-lock recovery, bounded timeout, per-process temporary files, and atomic replacement. Failure of this best-effort auxiliary history cannot fail the scientific simulation.

title: Qualifying Rain-Producing Experiments and Letting the Server Work Overnight
text:
A runnable marine OFAT showcase
marine_showcase_ofat_v1.yaml demonstrates the complete workflow in a collision-ON, rain-producing profile:
10 one-factor-at-reference cases
× 3 common random seeds
× control / seeding
= 60 physical PySDM executions
It varies dry radius, κ, number concentration, injection start time, and collision OFF/ON using a 5 s timestep and 800 background and seeding super-droplets. It is explicitly labeled exploratory physical sensitivity. Absolute parcel rain state is qualified; the quantitative seeding-minus-control response is not.

title: Qualifying Rain-Producing Experiments and Letting the Server Work Overnight
text:
Qualification must remain plural
The Results Dashboard and portable reports now separate absolute-state and seeding-response families, physical rain gates, paired-seed coverage, execution backend, child peak RSS, member-boundary RSS/USS trends, raw checkpoints, and subprocess failures.
A passing absolute state no longer turns an entire experiment into one green badge. Each metric family records what is supported and what remains not_supported_for_profile.
Final validation passed 37 unit/integration tests, including real PySDM products, control–seeding execution, detached workers, a two-worker sweep, failed-subprocess evidence, legacy migration, path budgets, key Streamlit AppTests, and the Results Dashboard. The remaining operational step is an actual Linux lab-server smoke test.
PR #3 attached provenance and scope to every result. PR #4 applied that principle to real rain production and persistent server execution. Its most important result is not +2.98%; it is the durable evidence that this number must not yet be presented as a converged quantitative seeding claim.

title: Turning PySDM Experiment Scripts into a Seeding Lab
text:
The first obstacle in building PySDM cloud-seeding sensitivity experiments was not a microphysical equation. Every change in conditions required editing Python, remembering which configuration produced which result directory, and reconstructing how a figure had been made. The simulations ran, but the experimental history was fragile.
PySDM-Seeding-Lab PR #2, merged on 13 July 2026, was the first attempt to turn those scripts into a scenario-based experimental platform. Across 31 commits and 66 changed files, the goal was to keep the question, configuration, execution, and result connected.

title: Turning PySDM Experiment Scripts into a Seeding Lab
text:
The starting problem
Manual scripts worked for one or two tests. They became unreliable as dry radius, hygroscopicity, injection timing, updraft, and random seeds multiplied.

Results did not identify the configuration that created them.
Control and seeding settings had to be synchronized by hand.
A small sweep change could silently create hundreds of model executions.
Long runs gave little indication of the current case or member.
Dashboard figures could outlive the context needed to interpret them.

The project target therefore became more specific than “build a GUI”: preserve one scientific question as one scenario.

title: Turning PySDM Experiment Scripts into a Seeding Lab
text:
Scenario as the experimental unit
The new workflow follows a deliberate sequence:
Create scenario
→ configure environment / aerosol / seeding / dynamics
→ configure parameter sweep
→ run simulation
→ inspect results through dashboard
A YAML scenario stores a name, slug, memo, timestamp, and complete configuration. Settings pages can update the working configuration or a selected saved scenario. Result directories include the scenario slug, making it possible to navigate from output back to experimental intent.
results/20260713_XXXXXX_dry_radius_kappa_sweep_parameter_sweep/
The Streamlit pages were reordered to match the research process:
00. Experiment Scenarios
01. Atmospheric Environment
02. Background Aerosol Settings
03. Seeding Particle Settings
04. Dynamic Parameters
05. Parameter Sweep
06. Run Simulation
07. Results Dashboard
The UI became a checklist: define the environment and background first, then seeding and dynamics, and only then choose what to vary.

title: Turning PySDM Experiment Scripts into a Seeding Lab
text:
Control, seeding, sweep, and ensemble
Seeding cannot be interpreted from a treatment run alone. Comparison mode creates matched control and seeding outputs:
control/
seeding/
comparison.csv
summary.json
metadata.json
config.yaml
For each variable, the result stores control, seeding, difference, and relative change. The first sweep catalog covered dry radius, \(\kappa\), injection start and duration, updraft velocity, and collision ON/OFF. Before execution, the app estimates
parameter combinations × ensemble members × control/seeding.
This is both a planning feature and a safety check against accidentally launching an oversized workload.
The Results Dashboard connects single, comparison, sweep, and ensemble results. Growth Pathway Diagnostics follows
vapour / supersaturation
→ cloud water
→ activated particles
→ size growth
→ rain water.
Sweep filters, full-range case sampling, and injection-relative time alignment were added so later parameter values would not disappear merely because a plot had a maximum case count.

title: Turning PySDM Experiment Scripts into a Seeding Lab
text:
Failures that changed the design
Renaming Streamlit pages left duplicate files and caused Multiple Pages specified with URL pathname run. A cleanup script and integrity check were added instead of relying on manual deletion.
During long sweeps, the dashboard sometimes read a CSV while it was still being written, producing EmptyDataError. Safe reading and incomplete-result filtering separated “directory exists” from “result is complete.” A subsequent regression made safe_read_csv() call itself recursively. The repair changed it back to pd.read_csv(path) and strengthened the integrity check to reject the pattern in future.
The lesson was larger than exception handling: dashboard stability comes from making known failures testable.

title: Turning PySDM Experiment Scripts into a Seeding Lab
section: What this stage achieved—and what it did not
text:
What this stage achieved—and what it did not







Before
After PR #2




Edit scripts for each condition
Preserve question and configuration in YAML scenarios


Manually track result folders
Link folders to scenario slugs and metadata


Focus on single runs
Support comparison, sweep, and ensemble workflows


Inspect final curves
Follow process pathways and uncertainty


Wait without context
Report case- and member-level progress



One important limitation remained. Some Growth Pathway columns were proxies inferred when the adapter did not expose native PySDM products. They were useful for validating the workflow, but they were not yet safe to interpret as direct physical output.
That limitation defined the next development question: how can every plotted diagnostic disclose whether it is native, derived, proxied, or missing?

title: Using WRF to Ask Where and How Widely Hygroscopic Seeding Should Occur
text:
Lin et al. (2023) couple WDM6 bulk microphysics with 43 CCN size bins and apply the hybrid WDM6–NCU scheme to a real Taiwanese stratocumulus case (Lin et al. 2023). The experiments ask where, over what area, and with which sizes hygroscopic particles should be released.
Read the paper

title: Using WRF to Ask Where and How Widely Hygroscopic Seeding Should Occur
text:
Hybrid microphysics
Bulk schemes are efficient but cannot preserve a detailed seeding aerosol spectrum. Full bin schemes are expensive in high-resolution real-case WRF. WDM6–NCU retains bulk cloud and rain while resolving CCN radii from \(0.001\) to \(20\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) in 43 bins. A measured trimodal flare distribution is used rather than one mean size.
The WRF 3.9.1 setup includes a 333 m inner LES domain. Sensitivity experiments vary release altitude (500, 1000, 1300, and 2200 m), treated area (1–100 km²), concentration, and particle-size range.

title: Using WRF to Ask Where and How Widely Hygroscopic Seeding Should Occur
text:
Three findings
Altitude. Release at 1300 m, inside the cloud, was most effective. Particles encountered supersaturation and liquid water quickly. Cloud-base particles were diluted and less consistently overlapped the target. For this stratiform case, the authors recommend in-cloud regions above 0.5% supersaturation and \(0.6\ \mathrm{g\,m^{-3}}\) liquid water; the latter is close to a \(0.5\ \mathrm{g\,m^{-3}}\) threshold in earlier work.
Area. Enhancement initially increased with treated area, then saturated around 40–60 km² because available cloud water became limiting. Total response and efficiency per unit material or area should therefore be reported together.
Process. Cloud-base release sometimes strengthened autoconversion, but the added precipitation was most closely associated with stronger accretion of cloud water by rain (\(P_{racw}\)). Seeding particles larger than roughly \(0.4\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) contributed most in these experiments.

title: Using WRF to Ask Where and How Widely Hygroscopic Seeding Should Occur
text:
Limits and next tests
The thresholds come from one cloud case. The hybrid scheme loses some spectral information after activation, plume dispersion remains uncertain, and a model CTRL–SEED difference is not observational proof of field enhancement.
WRF ensembles should test whether the area saturation persists across clouds, backgrounds, and physics options. PySDM can then resolve how each mode of the flare distribution changes activation and collision–coalescence along the same trajectories.
The most useful operational product would overlay three maps: seeding-particle residence time, supersaturation plus liquid water, and accretion response. Their intersection—not the widest release area—is the physically meaningful target.

title: Using WRF to Ask Where and How Widely Hygroscopic Seeding Should Occur
text:
References


Lin, Kai-I, Kao-Shen Chung, Sheng-Hsiang Wang, et al. 2023. “Evaluation of Hygroscopic Cloud Seeding in Warm-Rain Processes by a Hybrid Microphysics Scheme Using a Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) Model: A Real Case Study.” Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics 23: 10423–38. https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-23-10423-2023.

title: Can Negative Ions Enhance Rain? Revisiting China’s First Field Trial
text:
Zheng et al. (2021) evaluated high-voltage corona-discharge ion generators at Wushaoling and the Liupan Mountains from July to November 2020 (Zheng et al. 2021). Seven analyses were used to test whether charged aerosols transported from the ground altered clouds and rainfall.
Read the paper

title: Can Negative Ions Enhance Rain? Revisiting China’s First Field Trial
section: Three links the hypothesis must establish
text:
Three links the hypothesis must establish
The proposed mechanism contains three distinct claims:

Device: the generator produces a substantial ion perturbation.
Cloud: ions or charged aerosols reach cloud level and alter microphysics.
Rainfall: that cloud response exceeds natural variability and increases precipitation.

Strong evidence for one link does not automatically establish the next.

title: Can Negative Ions Enhance Rain? Revisiting China’s First Field Trial
text:
Field design and evidence
Wushaoling used 14 ON and 13 OFF days with random operation. Liupan operated more continuously and used network outages as controls, making its comparison weaker. The paper combined neural-network prediction, historical comparisons, ON/OFF days, spatial interpolation, upwind–downwind contrasts, ion measurements, and all-sky imagery.
Ion concentrations near the generators changed with very small p-values, supporting the device link. Some monthly all-sky metrics also increased, with several comparisons below \(p=0.02\). These are interesting intermediate observations, but the study did not directly measure the vertical profile of charged aerosols or cloud-droplet size distributions.
Rainfall estimates generally pointed in the hypothesized direction. A machine-learning counterfactual was about 21% below observed mean rainfall, while downwind rainfall exceeded upwind rainfall by about 58% at Wushaoling and 19% at Liupan. Yet major rainfall comparisons had p-values around 0.29–0.46. The sample was too small and natural rainfall variance too large for a precise causal estimate.

title: Can Negative Ions Enhance Rain? Revisiting China’s First Field Trial
section: Why seven methods are not seven independent experiments
text:
Why seven methods are not seven independent experiments
Most analyses reuse the same four-month weather record. A seasonal anomaly can therefore appear in several indicators at once. A well-fitting neural network also does not guarantee a valid counterfactual for unusual 2020 conditions. At Liupan, the lack of strict randomization creates additional confounding.
A stronger follow-up would use preregistered randomized ON/OFF schedules over multiple seasons, blinded operation, direct vertical measurements by drones or aircraft, and simultaneous cloud-droplet spectra and liquid-water observations. The analysis should follow the mediation chain from device to transport, microphysics, and rainfall.
The defensible conclusion is not “negative ions increase rain by 20%.” It is that the device and some cloud proxies changed, rainfall responses had a consistent direction, and the short, partially randomized trial could not yet isolate the rainfall effect from natural variability.

title: Can Negative Ions Enhance Rain? Revisiting China’s First Field Trial
text:
References


Zheng, Wei, Hengben Ma, Ming Zhang, et al. 2021. “Evaluation of the First Negative Ion-Based Cloud Seeding and Rain Enhancement Trial in China.” Water 13 (18): 2473. https://doi.org/10.3390/w13182473.

title: In Orographic Seeding, Overlap Matters More Than Dose
text:
Geresdi et al. (2020) simulated four real Wyoming Weather Modification Pilot Project cases using three-dimensional WRF and bin microphysics (Geresdi et al. 2020). The practical question is not merely whether AgI can nucleate ice, but when that first response survives the full path to additional surface precipitation.
Read the paper

title: In Orographic Seeding, Overlap Matters More Than Dose
text:
Why three dimensions matter
In a two-dimensional cross-section, seeding material cannot disperse laterally. In three dimensions, terrain and boundary-layer turbulence spread the plume both horizontally and vertically. The peak AgI concentration can therefore be roughly an order of magnitude lower for the same release rate. A response that appears strong in 2-D may be diluted in a real mountain flow.
Three-dimensional transport can also help by steering a plume into a liquid-water-rich region. Generator placement should therefore be evaluated by the trajectory from source to target, not by elevation alone.

title: In Orographic Seeding, Overlap Matters More Than Dose
text:
Horizontal liquid water path
The authors propose the horizontal liquid water path (h-LWP): liquid water integrated along the flow followed by the plume and growing particles.

Case-based interpretation of h-LWP






Maximum h-LWP
Simulated tendency




\(<0.1\ \mathrm{mm}\)
Negligible enhancement


Around \(0.5\ \mathrm{mm}\) or more
Enhancement near or above 5% becomes possible


\(>1.0\ \mathrm{mm}\)
More substantial enhancement if growth time is available



These are not universal thresholds; they are diagnostic ranges from four cases. Their value is conceptual: “the cloud contains liquid water” becomes the testable question “how much liquid water lies along the plume trajectory?”

title: In Orographic Seeding, Overlap Matters More Than Dose
text:
Following the microphysical chain
Seeding first increased pristine ice and vapor deposition. Aggregation and riming then transferred mass into snow. Surface enhancement appeared only when diffusional growth and/or riming continued. Increasing ice number alone was not a success metric: early ice production could consume liquid water and leave too little for later growth.
The paper therefore supports a process checklist:

Did AgI reach the intended cloud volume?
Was sufficient supercooled liquid water present there?
Did ice grow through deposition, aggregation, or riming?
Did the added mass survive transport and reach the surface?

title: In Orographic Seeding, Overlap Matters More Than Dose
text:
What remains uncertain
Four cases cannot establish a general effect size, and the CTRL–SEED difference depends on modeled natural precipitation and ice nucleation. The study is strongest as a physical explanation of success and failure, not as a universal percentage claim.
For future PySDM and WRF experiments, the most useful outputs are plume–liquid-water overlap, residence time, ice and snow mass budgets, and the lag between nucleation and surface flux. The main lesson is simple: cloud seeding is a placement and timing problem before it is a dosage problem.

title: In Orographic Seeding, Overlap Matters More Than Dose
text:
References


Geresdi, István, Lulin Xue, Noémi Sarkadi, and Roy Rasmussen. 2020. “Evaluation of Orographic Cloud Seeding Using a Bin Microphysics Scheme: Three-Dimensional Simulation of Real Cases.” Journal of Applied Meteorology and Climatology 59 (9): 1537–53. https://doi.org/10.1175/JAMC-D-19-0278.1.

title: About
text:
Jinu’s Cloud Seeding Blog is an open research notebook for learning and designing cloud-seeding research. It connects particle-based cloud microphysics with PySDM, mesoscale weather simulations with WRF, and reviews of the relevant literature in one research workflow.
Rather than presenting only finished conclusions, it records:

the physical question that started each experiment,
the assumptions and settings used,
how the code and results can be reproduced, and
what was learned when results differed from expectations.

title: Article Review
text:
Rather than summarizing conclusions alone, each review separates the research question, method, key assumptions, observations or model data, reproducible elements, and remaining limitations. Ideas found in the literature will feed back into PySDM or WRF experiments.
The collection currently covers seven papers, from glaciogenic, hygroscopic, and negative-ion seeding to effect accounting, numerical evaluation, and how seeding-particle size flips precipitation from suppression to enhancement. Each review separates what the paper demonstrates from what remains unproven.



2026-09-10 · Jinu


Same Mass, Different Size: When Hygroscopic Seeding Suppresses or Enhances Rain
Equal-mass KCl seeding in a 2-D bin model: a critical diameter sets the sign of the rain response and shrinks as the background gets more polluted.




2026-07-15 · Jinu


Using WRF to Ask Where and How Widely Hygroscopic Seeding Should Occur
Altitude, treated area, particle size, and the warm-rain process chain in a hybrid WDM6–CCN-bin model.




2026-07-15 · Jinu


Connecting Aerosol Hygroscopicity and CCN Activity with One κ
The κ-Köhler equation, mixture rule, limitations, and a direct connection to PySDM experiments.




2026-05-20 · Jinu


Can Negative Ions Enhance Rain? Revisiting China’s First Field Trial
Separating evidence for device operation, cloud response, and rainfall causality.




2026-05-20 · Jinu


The Principle Behind Fifty Years of Cloud Seeding: Close the Physical Chain
Opportunity windows and failure modes for static, dynamic, and hygroscopic seeding.




2026-04-08 · Jinu


In Orographic Seeding, Overlap Matters More Than Dose
How an AgI plume, supercooled liquid water, and growth time must overlap in 3-D terrain.




2026-04-08 · Jinu


How Much Additional Water Did Cloud Seeding Produce?
An accounting framework for converting rainfall-depth estimates into total water mass.

title: Experiments
text: This series begins with super-droplet representation, then moves through seeded-particle properties, background aerosol environments, and a κ–radius–timing response surface, before turning to updraft–timing regimes, terminal-velocity sensitivity, and a paper replication. Every note separates the question, baseline, changed conditions, diagnostics, limitations, and next hypothesis.

title: How Much Additional Water Did Cloud Seeding Produce?
text:
Ro et al. (2023) combine numerical winds, radar, and rain gauges to estimate cloud-seeding enhancement and convert millimeters of rain into total water mass (Ro et al. 2023). This translation is useful for applications such as wildfire prevention and drought response, but it also magnifies every assumption made upstream.
Read the paper

title: How Much Additional Water Did Cloud Seeding Produce?
text:
The calculation
The study defines a seeding box (SB) along the estimated material trajectory and a non-seeding box (NB) intended to represent natural precipitation. Enhanced rainfall is
\[
ER=CAR_{SB}-CAR_{NB},
\]
where \(CAR\) is area-mean cumulative rainfall. Total additional water is then
\[
TAER=ER\times ERA\times\rho_w,
\]
with \(ERA\) the affected area and \(\rho_w\) the density of water.

Reported estimates for the three cases


Case
Estimated enhancement
Total additional water




Wildfire prevention, AgI
1.74 mm
4.75 million t


Drought mitigation, CaCl₂
0.84 mm
1.30 million t


Dust reduction, CaCl₂
2.78 mm
24.44 million t



The dust case has the largest total mainly because its estimated effect area is wide. “Most effective” is therefore ambiguous unless the metric—rainfall depth, fractional change, affected area, total mass, or efficiency per unit material—is stated.

title: How Much Additional Water Did Cloud Seeding Produce?
text:
Strengths and limitations
The framework exposes the treatment area, comparison area, and conversion into mass. It also uses spatial information rather than a single before–after gauge. That transparency is valuable.
Its weak point is the counterfactual. Rainfall in NB may not equal the rainfall SB would have received without seeding. Terrain, moving rainbands, land–sea flow, radar errors, and uncertainty in modeled trajectories can all create SB–NB differences. Because \(TAER\) is a product of depth and area, small biases can become millions of tonnes.
A stronger analysis would repeat the calculation across multiple NB placements, effect-area boundaries, radar-error assumptions, and wind ensembles. It would report a distribution rather than one point estimate.
Most importantly, two questions should remain separate:

Did seeding cause a detectable precipitation change?
Conditional on that conclusion, how large was the added water volume?

Randomization, independent controls, physical tracers, or a complete microphysical response chain are needed for the first question. This paper provides a useful framework for the second.

title: How Much Additional Water Did Cloud Seeding Produce?
text:
References


Ro, Yonghun, Ki-Ho Chang, Sanghee Chae, Yun-Kyu Lim, Jung Mo Ku, and Woonseon Jung. 2023. “Estimation of the Total Amount of Enhanced Rainfall for a Cloud Seeding Experiment: Case Studies of Preventing Forest Fire, Drought, and Dust.” Advances in Meteorology 2023: 5478666. https://doi.org/10.1155/2023/5478666.

title: The Principle Behind Fifty Years of Cloud Seeding: Close the Physical Chain
text:
Bruintjes (1999) reviews decades of precipitation-enhancement experiments across static glaciogenic, dynamic, and hygroscopic seeding (Bruintjes 1999). Its durable message is methodological: a statistical rainfall difference must be supported by evidence for the physical chain that produced it.
Read the paper

title: The Principle Behind Fifty Years of Cloud Seeding: Close the Physical Chain
text:
Three strategies, three bottlenecks
Static glaciogenic seeding adds ice nuclei to supercooled clouds. It requires sufficient liquid water, suitable temperature, limited natural ice, accurate plume delivery, and enough time for deposition and riming. Orographic experiments often failed because liquid water and plume transport varied rapidly.
Dynamic seeding attempts rapid glaciation and latent-heating feedback:
\[
\begin{gathered}
\text{seeding}\rightarrow\text{glaciation}\rightarrow\text{latent heat} \\
\rightarrow\text{updraft}\rightarrow\text{cloud growth}\rightarrow\text{rain}
\end{gathered}
\]
The possible amplification is large, but every arrow must exceed the already large natural variability of convective clouds.
Hygroscopic seeding introduces salt particles to broaden the initial droplet spectrum and accelerate collision–coalescence. Flare-generated submicron particles renewed interest after earlier delivery problems. Yet maritime clouds with abundant natural giant CCN may already be efficient, leaving little room for improvement.

Comparing strategies by bottleneck rather than material







Strategy
Intended bottleneck
Key failure mode




Static glaciogenic
Too few ice nuclei
Poor plume–liquid-water overlap


Dynamic
Weak or short-lived convection
Long causal chain and large natural variance


Hygroscopic
Slow warm-rain coalescence
Already-efficient clouds or poor particle delivery

title: The Principle Behind Fifty Years of Cloud Seeding: Close the Physical Chain
section: The “new prospects” that became standard tools
text:
The “new prospects” that became standard tools
The review highlighted multiparameter radar, lidar, satellite microphysics, aircraft observations, tracers such as SF₆ and chaff, and time-dependent 3-D models. These tools are now much more capable, but they still answer the same questions: Where did the material go? Was the cloud seedable? What changed first? Did that response reach the surface? Could natural variability produce the same signal?
Bruintjes also warns against overselling early hygroscopic results. Cloud seeding had already lost credibility through claims that outran evidence. Negative cases are scientifically useful when the failed link is identified in advance.
For numerical work, this means saving more than final precipitation. Plume position, activation, hydrometeor spectra, water budgets, process rates, and surface fluxes should form a traceable chain. Statistics and physics are complementary requirements, not substitutes.

title: The Principle Behind Fifty Years of Cloud Seeding: Close the Physical Chain
text:
References


Bruintjes, Roelof T. 1999. “A Review of Cloud Seeding Experiments to Enhance Precipitation and Some New Prospects.” Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society 80 (5): 805–20. https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0477(1999)080<0805:AROCSE>2.0.CO;2.

title: Connecting Aerosol Hygroscopicity and CCN Activity with One κ
text:
Petters & Kreidenweis (2007) compress aerosol water uptake and cloud-condensation-nucleus activity into one hygroscopicity parameter, \(\kappa\) (Petters and Kreidenweis 2007). The result is not chemistry-free physics, but a practical bridge between subsaturated growth measurements and supersaturated activation.
Read the paper

title: Connecting Aerosol Hygroscopicity and CCN Activity with One κ
text:
The κ-Köhler equation
For dry diameter \(D_d\) and wet diameter \(D\),
\[
S(D)=\frac{D^3-D_d^3}{D^3-D_d^3(1-\kappa)}
\exp\left(\frac{A}{D}\right),
\qquad
A=\frac{4\sigma_{s/a}M_w}{RT\rho_w}.
\]
The first factor represents the solute effect; the exponential is the Kelvin curvature term. Larger \(\kappa\) implies stronger water uptake and activation at lower critical supersaturation. \(\kappa=0\) approaches a non-hygroscopic particle.

Typical ranges summarized in the paper


Material class
Representative \(\kappa\) range




Non-hygroscopic
Near 0


Organics
0.01–0.5


Atmospheric aerosol
0.1–0.9


Inorganic salts
0.5–1.4



For an internally mixed particle, a simple volume-weighted rule is
\[
\kappa_{mix}=\sum_i\varepsilon_i\kappa_i.
\]
This turns composition into an activation parameter without a full activity model.

title: Connecting Aerosol Hygroscopicity and CCN Activity with One κ
text:
What one parameter misses
A constant \(\kappa\) cannot fully represent surfactant-driven surface-tension changes, limited solubility, crystallization and deliquescence hysteresis, liquid–liquid phase separation, size-dependent composition, or externally mixed populations. It is a baseline model, not a replacement for detailed thermodynamics when those effects control the question.

title: Connecting Aerosol Hygroscopicity and CCN Activity with One κ
text:
A PySDM experiment
With a fixed dry-size distribution and number concentration, vary \(\kappa\) across 0.1, 0.3, 0.6, and 1.0 under the same updraft. Record critical supersaturation, activated fraction, peak supersaturation, cloud-droplet number, mean radius, and time to collision–coalescence. Then vary size and \(\kappa\) together.
That second step matters because a large, moderately hygroscopic particle may activate more readily than a small, highly hygroscopic one. Hygroscopic-seeding performance depends on the combination of size, number, \(\kappa\), and updraft—not on chemistry alone.

title: Connecting Aerosol Hygroscopicity and CCN Activity with One κ
text:
References


Petters, M. D., and S. M. Kreidenweis. 2007. “A Single Parameter Representation of Hygroscopic Growth and Cloud Condensation Nucleus Activity.” Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics 7: 1961–71. https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-7-1961-2007.

title: Same Mass, Different Size: When Hygroscopic Seeding Suppresses or Enhances Rain
text:
Ren et al. (2025) use the two-dimensional slab-symmetric bin-microphysics model of Tel Aviv University to simulate a warm convective cloud over Sanya, Hainan, China, on 11 May 2024. Keeping the total seeding mass fixed, they inject single-diameter KCl particles from 0.1 to 90 µm (Ren et al. 2025). The question: with the same amount of material, can particle size alone decide whether rain decreases or increases, and where is the boundary? I presented this paper at our lab meeting on 10 September 2026.
Read the paper

title: Same Mass, Different Size: When Hygroscopic Seeding Suppresses or Enhances Rain
section: The question: what must be fixed to see a size effect?
text:
The question: what must be fixed to see a size effect?
Earlier studies proposed very different “optimal seed sizes”: 0.5–6 µm, 1.5–2.5 µm, or larger than 10 µm. The authors attribute this to different background aerosols and seed spectra across studies, and to the inherently nonlinear rain response to CCN. So they fix the background and scan size alone. There are three questions.

At equal total seeding mass, does the seed diameter suppress or enhance precipitation?
Is there a critical diameter at which the sign flips?
How does that critical diameter move with background aerosol?

The key device is mass-conserved monodisperse seeding. The seed spectrum from the South African hygroscopic-flare experiments is used only as a total-mass reference; for each target diameter, the particle number is back-calculated to give that mass.
\[
N(D)=\frac{M_{\mathrm{seed}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{s}}\,\frac{\pi}{6}D^{3}}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
N(D)=N(0.1\,\mu\mathrm{m})\left(\frac{0.1\,\mu\mathrm{m}}{D}\right)^{3}
\]
In words: “the number of seeds equals the total mass divided by the mass of one seed.” \(M_{\mathrm{seed}}\) is the fixed total seeding mass, \(\rho_{\mathrm{s}}\) the KCl density, and \(\frac{\pi}{6}D^3\) the volume of a sphere of diameter \(D\). Because the mass of one particle scales with \(D^3\), the number falls as \(D^{-3}\). The seed concentrations in the paper’s Table 2 follow exactly this ratio: \(5.45\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) at 0.1 µm, \(5.45\times10^{2}\) at 1 µm, \(5.45\times10^{-1}\) at 10 µm, and \(7.48\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) at 90 µm. A tenfold larger diameter means a thousandfold fewer particles. This size–number trade-off is the key to reading every result below.

title: Same Mass, Different Size: When Hygroscopic Seeding Suppresses or Enhances Rain
text:
Model and experimental design

Model setup (paper, Section 2)






Item
Setting




Model
Tel Aviv University 2D slab-symmetric spectral bin-microphysics model (Yin et al., 2000); winds from the vorticity–stream-function formulation


Grid and domain
\(\Delta x=\Delta z=300\) m, 30 km wide, model top 12 km


Time
2.5 s for condensation/evaporation, 5 s for other processes, 40 min integration


Hydrometeor bins
cloud drops, ice crystals, graupel, snow, each 34 mass bins (mass doubling between bins); liquid bins span 3.125–8064 µm in diameter


CCN bins
natural CCN in 67 bins (minimum radius \(4.1\times10^{-3}\) µm) plus a separate seed spectrum with its own prognostic equation


Materials
natural CCN = (NH₄)₂SO₄, seed = KCl


Case and initial state
warm convective cloud near Sanya around 14:00 Beijing Time on 2024-05-11; 12:00 Sanya radiosonde (WMO 59948); surface about 980 hPa, LCL about 900 m, 0 °C level about 5.5 km


Convective trigger
thermal bubble at 900 m in the domain centre, maximum +3 °C




Seeding design (paper, Sections 3.2 and 4.5)






Item
Setting




Time and place
10 min into the run, a single level at cloud base (900 m), central three grid columns (900 m)


Procedure
one release every 60 s (each within one 5 s dynamical step), five releases over 5 min; control volume 900 m × 300 m × 300 m (300 m width normal to the model plane assumed)


Size experiments
C00 (unseeded) + 27 runs: 0.1–0.9 µm (C01–C09), 1–9 µm (C11–C19), 10–90 µm (C21–C29)


Background aerosol
Jaenicke three-mode maritime, continental, urban; maximum cloud-drop number about 140, 400, 1400 cm⁻³ (Section 2.2)



The unseeded run C00 starts raining at about 15 min, peaks once at 23–24 min, and stops at about 35 min: a single-peaked episode of roughly 20 minutes. The cloud lies mainly between 1 and 4 km, below the 0 °C level, so although the model carries ice categories, in this case essentially only warm processes operate.

title: Same Mass, Different Size: When Hygroscopic Seeding Suppresses or Enhances Rain
section: Result 2: sharing the vapour versus building large collectors
text:
Result 2: sharing the vapour versus building large collectors
A hygroscopic seed acts in two directions. Activated seeds take up vapour and hold back the activation and growth of natural CCN (competition for vapour), and seeds that grow large sweep up the surrounding cloud drops (collector effect). Under equal mass, the diameter decides which one wins.
Sub-micrometer (0.1–0.9 µm). Many small seeds activate → many drops share the vapour → the number spectrum peak shifts to smaller diameters, and 20–40 µm drops and the mass above 10 µm decrease → the maximum collision–coalescence rate in the cloud core is actually earlier and larger → but drops do not reach raindrop size, so surface rain falls. Onset and end times match C00; only the peak drops. Collisions are frequent but mass growth is blocked, which amounts to injecting polluted air.
Giant (1–9 µm). Few seeds, so the spectrum below 10 µm is nearly identical to C00 → from 2 µm (C12) the number and mass of drops above 10 µm increase, most strongly at 7–9 µm → between 18 and 21 min, mass below 30 µm shifts to larger sizes → the collision–coalescence peak leads the rain peak by 3–4 min and grows → surface rain increases. At 1 µm (C11) there are slightly fewer large drops than in C00, so it is still on the suppression side.
Ultra-giant (10–90 µm). Each seed is immediately a large collector → the collision–coalescence peak comes 3–5 min earlier than in C00 and is much larger → rain onset and peak move earlier (earlier for larger diameters). Beyond 60 µm, however, there are too few seeds → too few collectors → smaller enhancement. From 20 to 90 µm the number drops by a factor of about 91. In the spectra, 40–1000 µm drops are more abundant for smaller seeds and drops above 1000 µm for larger seeds.

title: Same Mass, Different Size: When Hygroscopic Seeding Suppresses or Enhances Rain
section: Result 3: the more polluted, the smaller the critical diameter
text:
Result 3: the more polluted, the smaller the critical diameter
The authors repeated giant-range seeding under three background aerosols.

Critical diameter by background aerosol (paper, Section 4.5 and Conclusions)








Background
Max cloud-drop number (cm⁻³)
Critical diameter
Response




Maritime (M)
140 (Sec. 2.2) / 120 (Sec. 4.5)
about 6 µm
clear suppression only at 1 µm; otherwise small


Continental (C)
400 / 450
about 3 µm
clearer than maritime


Urban (U)
1400
about 2 µm
clearest; strongest enhancement after the flip



The authors’ explanation: clean cloud → few natural drops, and condensation alone already makes fairly large drops → a seed must be several micrometres to make a difference. Polluted cloud → many drops and a narrow spectrum → even a 2 µm seed starts collision–coalescence quickly. In my own words: to matter as a “large drop”, a seed must be larger than its neighbours, and the background aerosol sets that bar.






WarningInconsistencies I found while reading




The text of Section 4.5 calls the thresholds a “radius of about 6 and 3 µm”, while the Figure 11 caption and the Conclusions call the same values a diameter. Since the experimental variable is diameter, I read them as diameters.
Section 4.1 gives 30 µm as the optimal ultra-giant size; Table 2, Section 4.4, the Conclusions, and the Abstract give 60 µm. The Table 2 maximum (+192.34%) is at 60 µm.
Section 3.1 describes C00 as an urban background and Conclusion (2) gives “about 2 µm under the present polluted background”, but Section 4.5 calls the same experiments the continental C series (critical about 3 µm). The Table 2 flip (1→2 µm) matches the urban value. The maximum cloud-drop numbers also differ between Sections 2.2 and 4.5.
Section 4.4 says the number falls “by a factor of about 27” from 10 to 60 µm, but at equal mass it is \((60/10)^3=216\), which the Table 2 values also give. A factor of 27 corresponds to 10→30 µm.

title: Same Mass, Different Size: When Hygroscopic Seeding Suppresses or Enhances Rain
section: Why it matters for my research
text:
Why it matters for my research
A design that removes the dose confound. In a fixed-number design, enlarging the seed also raises the total mass as \(D^3\), so “larger seeds work better” gets mixed with “more material works better.” The equal-mass design removes this confound. In exchange, size and number are tied by \(N\propto D^{-3}\), so the size effect here is the effect of how many pieces the same material is split into. It has the same structure as my Experiment 3, where large seeds were strongest under fixed number but a size–number trade-off appeared under fixed mass.
Coupling of κ and size. The paper explains the seed’s competitive advantage with Köhler theory: at equal size, KCl activates at a lower supersaturation than (NH₄)₂SO₄. In the language of my κ-Köhler review, the seed has both a larger dry size and a larger \(\kappa\) (Petters and Kreidenweis 2007). Because the paper fixes the material to KCl, the relative roles of \(\kappa\) and size remain an open question.
Accretion needs to be separated. Lin et al. (2023) diagnosed rain–cloud accretion as the main pathway to added rain from process rates (Lin et al. 2023). Ren et al. show only one total collision–coalescence rate, so we cannot tell whether giant and ultra-giant seeds advanced autoconversion or strengthened accretion. Also, Lin’s “larger than 0.4 µm” is a boundary within a trimodal flare distribution on radius bins, whereas Ren’s values are monodisperse diameters; the numbers should not be compared directly.
The physical chain. The chain emphasised by Bruintjes (1999), seed → drop spectrum → collision–coalescence → surface rain, is followed inside the model through spectra and collision rates (Bruintjes 1999). The last link, observational verification, is missing.

title: Same Mass, Different Size: When Hygroscopic Seeding Suppresses or Enhances Rain
section: Limitations: what was shown, and how far
text:
Limitations: what was shown, and how far

What is and is not supported






Category
Content




Supported by the results
size dependence of the sign (0.1–0.9 µm: 9/9 suppressed; 10–90 µm: 9/9 enhanced); critical diameter decreasing maritime > continental > urban


Descriptive values
−82%, +192%, the 60 µm optimum, the jagged magnitudes within 1–9 µm


Authors’ interpretation
vapour competition and collector shortage, inferred from spectra and the total collision–coalescence rate


Not shown
autoconversion/accretion split, supersaturation or condensation-rate diagnostics, ensemble spread, observational verification




One case, 2D, idealised. One Sanya sounding, 2D slab symmetry, a uniform lower boundary, a thermal bubble, and 40 min of integration. Generalisation to 3D clouds or other cloud systems was not shown.
One integration per configuration. Without an ensemble, the jaggedness within 1–9 µm (5 µm +24.11% → 6 µm +15.92% → 7 µm +74.70% → 8 µm +63.75%) cannot be separated into physical signal or numerical noise. The 60 µm optimum is also a single run (+192.34%) standing out while the other six runs from 30 to 90 µm cluster at +157–163%, so “saturation above 30 µm” is a safer reading than “optimal size.”
Resolution of the critical diameter. The 1–9 µm range was scanned in 1 µm steps, and the responses at 2–4 µm (+0.72, +0.53, +2.98%) are close to zero. “About 2 µm” is closer to “the sign flips between 1 and 2 µm and stays nearly neutral up to 4 µm.”
Monodisperse, single injection. Real flares produce broad distributions. Injection time (10 min), height (cloud base), and location were each tested once.
Missing processes. The authors note that entrainment–mixing and turbulence-enhanced collisions are absent and could change the quantitative response. The cloud stays below 0 °C, so ice processes were not tested.

title: Same Mass, Different Size: When Hygroscopic Seeding Suppresses or Enhances Rain
text:
Questions that lead to reproduction
I chose this paper because its questions are almost the same as those of my PySDM seeding experiments. Alongside the presentation, I started reproducing it along two paths.

0-D parcel reproduction. In Experiment 7 I recomputed the same equal-mass diameter scan under the three backgrounds with a PySDM parcel. A parcel has no surface rain, so I compared shifts in rain-onset time. The ordering of the critical diameter (maritime > continental > urban) matched the paper, but the values were about half of the paper’s, and the response sign agreed in 78 of 81 conditions (71/81 under the strict criterion where the confidence interval excludes zero).
2D reproduction. To build the same kind of 2D bin-microphysics setup in WRF, I am working through a tutorial track starting from microphysics schemes and fast SBM.

Four questions remain.

Do the 1–2 µm sign flip and the 60 µm optimum survive an ensemble that perturbs only the initial state?
If a broad flare-like distribution replaces the monodisperse seed, do the suppressing and enhancing modes cancel?
If the collision–coalescence rate is split into autoconversion and accretion, which one carries the ultra-giant enhancement?
Is the halved critical diameter in 0-D due to the structure of a parcel without sedimentation and dynamics, or to the microphysics settings?
